title: What Is the US Economy Trying to Tell Us?
description_html:
US economic growth is up but consumer sentiment is down. Another rate hike, expected this year, could help lower inflation, but do little to ease the frustrations of much of the middle class, for whom the American dream sits just out of reach.

On today’s Big Take podcast, editors Matthew Boesler and Cristina Lindblad join Sarah Holder to unpack what the data says is happening in the US economy and why consumer sentiment tells another story.

Read more: 

  • The Trump Stock Market Is Lousy for Most
  • US Consumer Prices Rise by Most Since April in Broad Advance

We have a special Bloomberg subscription offer for podcast listeners at Bloomberg.com/podcastoffer.

Host: Sarah Holder; Guests: Matthew Boesler and Cristina Lindblad; Produced by David Fox; Edited by Paddy Hirsch and Naomi Shavin; Engineering by Emma Munger.

If you have a job right now, you're doing fine.
And that's reflected in the low unemployment rate, the low layoff rate.
If you don't have a job right now, you're kind of locked out because the hiring rate is also extremely low.
The housing market, similar sort of thing.
If you have a house or if you had one, you know, before 2020, 2021, you're doing great.
You're seeing a lot of house price appreciation.
But as we know, if you don't have a house right now, you probably are struggling to get into that market because interest rates are so high and house prices are so high.
So we kind of have this situation where we do have a large group of people who are doing fine.
And we also have a large group of people who are kind of locked out of these like basic elements of the American dream, right?
You get a job, you get a house, you get a car.
And I think it helps explain why growth can be strong, but sentiment can be weak.
I'm Sarah Holder, and this is The Big Take from Bloomberg News.
Today on the show, Bloomberg's Matt Boesler and Christina Lindblad join me to unpack what the data says is happening in the U.S. economy and whether consumer sentiment tells another story.
The Big Take On the face of it, there are lots of positive things happening in the economy, right?

But there are also some not so good signals, including but not limited to the inflation data we got on Wednesday, which showed that the CPI is up 3.7 percent from last year, mostly driven by energy costs.
Christina, you edit global economic coverage for Businessweek.
What's flashing green and what's flashing red for you in the economy right now?
Well, flashing green is we still have a lot of momentum from this huge investment wave we're seeing in artificial intelligence.
And consumers have been more resilient for years now than people have expected them to be.
What's flashing red is money's getting more expensive. for different actors.
So the U.S. faces higher financing costs.
It's also affecting some of the hyperscalers and the companies that want to build all of these data centers.
Definitely prices. So the cost of living, which was something that Donald Trump ran on as being able to or trying to control is going higher.
And we can tell from polls that that's making people upset.
And I think you know, we were expecting maybe by this time this year that we were going to be seeing the housing market, you know, kind of unfreeze a bit.
And that's definitely not going in the right direction either.
Okay. I'm hearing on balance a bit more red flashing lights than green ones for you.
What about Matt from your perch covering the U.S. economy and the Fed?
What are you seeing?
Yeah, I think I would agree with a lot of what Christina said.
I think for me, it kind of all comes down to this AI data center build-out, right?
So as long as that continues, things can keep going the way they're going in a pretty self-sustaining fashion.

Consumer spending has been pretty strong, and we think a lot of that is upper-income consumers who are benefiting from these stock market gains that are, of course, being driven by the AI boom, right?
And so it's a narrow source of growth, but it's a pretty good source of growth for now.
And the question is, how long does that continue, right?
Just this week now, we're seeing a little bit of turmoil in the stock market.
You know, the question when that happens is always, is this just a temporary breather or is this investors really pulling forward the timeline for how long they think this can continue?
And so I think a lot of economists would say they see this continuing through maybe 2027 or 2028.
But of course, that's something that's just kind of impossible to forecast.
And so for me, it really all comes down to that.
Well, so let's dig into some of the economic data we got this week and last week.
So we got inflation data, the CPI up 3.7 percent, but we also got data on wage gains.
So the Trump administration has been talking up some encouraging recent wage growth numbers for Americans in blue collar jobs like manufacturing and construction.
What about the rest of the workforce?
What do we know?
Yeah, I mean, a lot of the job growth and the wage growth we are seeing is on that sort of goods producing side right now.
And I think a lot of us presume that that is really also being driven by the AI build out, right?
You have a ton of data center construction right now.
You have a lot of manufacturing for equipment that is going into those data centers.
And that's really keeping things afloat at a time when, as Christina said, the housing market is doing terrible.
So that's typically the source of job growth for those kinds of sectors.
Those sectors are sailing through that housing weakness because of the data center story, right?
On the services side, it's a lot slower.
The big standout on the services side, obviously, is healthcare.
That is something that has really been the major driver of job growth over the last several years.
But there too, we're starting to see a slowdown.
So That's a little worrying because if we lose that healthcare job growth driver, then we're not left with much else.
And so that's definitely something. that we need to keep an eye on.
And according to BLS data released this week, average weekly and hourly earnings decreased around 0.5% month over month, and they're down from last year as well.
How significant is this, Christina?

I think, of course, everyone is now looking at how real wages are performing, trying to figure out whether there is going to be consumer retrenchment, and that's going to be a concern. the prices of fuel have been so volatile and it looked like inflation, you know, was going to be back on track to descend.
And now this month with this new print, you know, it just, it looks less hopeful.
The picture looks so different than the beginning of the year.
And, you know, the war in Iran is one of the biggest factors for that.

We've, seen real wages declining all year since the Iran war started with this surge in energy prices, and now what looks to be broadening out in inflation, potentially because those higher energy prices are working their way into the cost of other goods and services.
But at the same time, we're still seeing pretty strong consumer spending.
So that's telling you that businesses are able to pass those costs along to consumers.
Consumers are still willing to pay those prices and continue to buy those things, even when the prices are going up and their purchasing power is being eroded.
And so to me, that kind of speaks to, yes, we have this supply shock that's driving up prices, but we also have strong demand that is keeping this whole thing going.
And so as long as we have that strong demand, that is something that potentially keeps inflation elevated in and of itself.
I mean, Kyla Scanlon, who has a gift for creating new words, launched a new one this week.
She calls it shrugflation.
And I thought, yes, that's sort of a good way for how we see a lot of consumers acting You know, that in polls and surveys, they're saying, I'm bothered by inflation.
It's, you know, money is tighter, but they continue and a lot of different income levels they continue to spend.

And I think, like Matt said, you also have to take into account the wealth effect that we've seen from like, you know, valuations of stocks shooting up from home prices continuing to go up in many parts of the country.
Yeah, the consumer spending data is pretty staggering.
Actual U.S. consumer spending hit a record high of $16.79 trillion in the second quarter, but the consumer sentiment index has been at or near record lows.
There is some shrugging going on for sure, but how do you explain that?
If you think about all the factors that would normally factor into how people see their own financial situation, there is data now showing that concerns about losing one's job or have risen.
And I think with AI, that that playing out in the background, that is affecting people's psychology and it's hard to ignore.
I mean, it's in the news all the time.

So if you're not worried about your own job, there was, I think, a very striking interview that I saw where they were going to, you know, red states and talking to people who voted for Trump in the last election.
And one gentleman who was older was a boomer was saying, I'm worried about my granddaughter.
You know, that she like graduated college and she can't find a job.
So even people who we know from all the data are in a pretty good place, which is that generation, you know, is worried about sort of like they're the people close to them.
And I think all of those things go and factor in into sentiment in a way that it doesn't in the hard data.
Yeah.
And beyond spending, Americans are also big borrowers.
Of course, we got some data from the New York Fed recently saying that household debt is actually flattening out right now.
It's down $13 billion in the second quarter.
What's behind that?
And is that a good sign?
Yeah, I think it is a good sign.
I mean, it's just, you know, the bottom line is that the economy right now is growing faster than debt.
And if you look at consumer credit, for example, as a share of GDP, it's actually at a like 26 or 27 year low, you know, so there's been a lot of broad-based deleveraging.
And I think a lot of that had to do with all of the money that was sent out during the pandemic in the form of the checks and also the expanded unemployment insurance benefits.

I mean, one of the most striking economic facts of that period was that household income actually went up During the pandemic recession, which is like, of course, something that's never happened before.
And, you know, that's all because of the money that the government pumped into the economy.
It allowed a lot of people to pay down debt.
That's something that we saw was a major rebound. of that.
So you still have that kind of long tail that has kept the debt lower than it would otherwise be.
At the same time, you also have a situation where the people who do have debt are increasingly falling behind on their payments.
So we're seeing delinquency rates going up, even if it's on this kind of smaller base, right, of debt.
And a lot of that obviously has to do with these really high interest rates that we have.
So if you don't have debt, you're doing great right now.
If you do have debt, you're starting to struggle.
More from my conversation with Matt and Christina after the break.
For the first time in a long time, it is a buyer's market.
Housing supply is rising.
Sellers have begun to outnumber buyers.
But at the same time, we're seeing this housing market freeze because mortgage rates are so elevated.
Pending home sales were at their lowest since 2014, according to data from Redfin on September, not counting the beginning of the 2020 pandemic, which was a whole other story.
But Christina, what are you seeing in the housing market and how do you explain what's going on there?
I just think mortgage rates have risen to a level where only real cash buyers and people who may be sizing down are able to break in.

And also, I mean, from one of the recent real estate stories that I edited, we looked at different communities and only in a few states where there is a government push to build starter homes, builders are starting to also tack away from that sector of the market towards higher end.
So in the US, I have to say, over the last few years, it seems like the story for for which kind of autos get billed, which kind of houses get billed.
It's about we're going to prioritize the higher income consumer because that's where the margins are and that's where the resilience is.
So I want to segue now to talk about the stock market a little bit because the stock market is doing very well.
The S & P is up more than 12% since the beginning of the year.
That's, of course, one of the big economic success stories that, again, the Trump administration has been touting heading into the midterms.
What is driving those gains?
Yeah, so of course, AI is the big story, right?
A few companies are doing extraordinarily well.
You're also seeing that filter through to a lot of like industrials and other sorts of companies that are supplying the AI boom, right?
The other big story, obviously, is energy right now because oil prices are so high.
The energy companies are making a lot of money off of this situation that we have with the war.
Beyond that, We kind of have a situation where most stocks are rising.
So there's like real breadth to the stock market rally, but a few stocks, those AI stocks, those energy stocks are just doing extraordinarily well.
So the concentration is like really in the gains as opposed to the breadth.
Now there's also interesting things going on on the consumer side that kind of tie back to our discussion about how consumers are doing.
There, you kind of see a split too, where the consumer stocks that are supplying energy high-end services, things like travel, the hotel stocks, they're generally doing well.

The consumer stocks like the Home Depots of the world, the home builders, and so on, anything that the auto companies, anything that is tied to interest rates and that sort of American dream kind of story, those are the stocks that are not doing well because people just can't afford to buy homes right now.
They can't afford to buy cars.
And I think you kind of see that split there where the upper income consumer is doing well and the more middle class consumer is doing less well.
The K-shaped economy showing up in the stock market.
Exactly.
This has been a topic of conversation for most of the year about how a very narrow group of companies are driving the performance and people...
Depending on the day of the week, go back and forth between I want to be fully exposed to this or I want to like go and look at my portfolio and make sure that I'm not overly exposed to this.
I mean, this week we saw in the semiconductor index a big decline and also it's down for the year as a whole, I think.
Right. It's nice to be exposed to it when it's having a good day.
Yeah.
And also we're talking about, you know, it's such a forward-looking industry.
I mean, the stock market's always more forward-looking than the, you know, economic indicators and often than not.
Right, it's betting on the future.
But this is like, you know, we're betting on a whole new technology that we don't even totally understand what it's good.
For, right? And it can be true, of course, that AI stocks are doing well, industrial stocks are doing well, stocks tied to high-end consumers are doing well.
And also true that If the AI boom fizzles out, then everything is going to be going down, right?
Because that's really like the first thing, right, in the chain.
Like that's the key thing that is kind of propelling the momentum for everyone forward right now.
I have to ask about the midterms because these elections are coming up in just 19 days at this point.
How is this all going to play for voters?

One data point on this that is really interesting to me is that if you look at some of the consumer sentiment surveys, like the University of Michigan survey, for example, they break out sentiment by Republican respondents versus Democratic respondents.
And it's certainly the case that sentiment among Republicans is still higher than it was during the Biden years.
But it's also a fair bit lower than it was during Trump's first term.
So that tells you that even sentiment among Republicans is not great right now.
And of course, that probably does connect back to what Christina was talking about with inflation.
It affects everyone.

And just the fact that the inflation that we're seeing right now can be tied so directly to very visible initiatives that President Trump has been out championing, first with tariffs and then with this war.

And it's easy to imagine a scenario where if he had just come into office and not done either of those things, Inflation might be at or even perhaps below 2% at the moment, and his popularity would be through the roof.
Yes, because the AI boom would be, you know, still be playing.
So my last question is about the Fed, because they have indicated that there will be one more rate hike this year, and there's one more meeting before the midterms.
What kind of impact could a rate decision from the Fed meeting have, both for the consumer and in terms of how it might motivate voters?

We really already have seen the impact of these rate hikes that the Fed is expected to do because they're already priced into the market, which means longer-term interest rates already reflect those expected rate hikes.
And so what we've seen in particular over the last, say, four, five, six weeks is a surge in mortgage rates as markets have come around to the view that the Fed is going to have to hike.
So they've gone from under 7% to up to 7.5% now.
And That's something that like we're not seeing in the monthly housing data yet because it comes out with like a month lag.

But we're very much expecting to see in upcoming reports on housing that this is just going to be another hammer blow for a market that was already severely depressed because rates were so high even before this latest mortgage rate shock.
This is The Big Take from Bloomberg News.
I'm Sarah Holder.
To get more from The Big Take and unlimited access to all of Bloomberg.com, subscribe today at Bloomberg.com slash podcast offer.
If you liked this episode, make sure to subscribe and review The Big Take wherever you listen to podcasts.
It helps people find the show.
Thanks for listening.
We'll be back tomorrow.

The consumer stocks like the Home Depots of the world, the home builders, and so on, anything that the auto companies, anything that is tied to interest rates and that sort of American dream kind of story, those are the stocks that are not doing well because people just can't afford to buy homes right now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They can't afford to buy cars. And I think you kind of see that split there where the upper income consumer is doing well and the more middle class consumer is doing less well.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: The K-shaped economy showing up in the stock market.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Exactly.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: This has been a topic of conversation for most of the year about how a very narrow group of companies are driving the performance and people... Depending on the day of the week, go back and forth between I want to be fully exposed to this or I want to like go and look at my portfolio and make sure that I'm not overly exposed to this. I mean, this week we saw in the semiconductor index a big decline and also it's down for the year as a whole, I think.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Right. It's nice to be exposed to it when it's having a good day.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And also we're talking about, you know, it's such a forward-looking industry. I mean, the stock market's always more forward-looking than the, you know, economic indicators and often than not.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Right, it's betting on the future.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: But this is like, you know, we're betting on a whole new technology that we don't even totally understand what it's good.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: For, right? And it can be true, of course, that AI stocks are doing well, industrial stocks are doing well, stocks tied to high-end consumers are doing well. And also true that If the AI boom fizzles out, then everything is going to be going down, right? Because that's really like the first thing, right, in the chain. Like that's the key thing that is kind of propelling the momentum for everyone forward right now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I have to ask about the midterms because these elections are coming up in just 19 days at this point. How is this all going to play for voters?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: One data point on this that is really interesting to me is that if you look at some of the consumer sentiment surveys, like the University of Michigan survey, for example, they break out sentiment by Republican respondents versus Democratic respondents. And it's certainly the case that sentiment among Republicans is still higher than it was during the Biden years. But it's also a fair bit lower than it was during Trump's first term.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So that tells you that even sentiment among Republicans is not great right now. And of course, that probably does connect back to what Christina was talking about with inflation. It affects everyone. And just the fact that the inflation that we're seeing right now can be tied so directly to very visible initiatives that President Trump has been out championing, first with tariffs and then with this war. And it's easy to imagine a scenario where if he had just come into office and not done either of those things, Inflation might be at or even perhaps below 2% at the moment, and his popularity would be through the roof.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yes, because the AI boom would be, you know, still be playing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So my last question is about the Fed, because they have indicated that there will be one more rate hike this year, and there's one more meeting before the midterms. What kind of impact could a rate decision from the Fed meeting have, both for the consumer and in terms of how it might motivate voters?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We really already have seen the impact of these rate hikes that the Fed is expected to do because they're already priced into the market, which means longer-term interest rates already reflect those expected rate hikes. And so what we've seen in particular over the last, say, four, five, six weeks is a surge in mortgage rates as markets have come around to the view that the Fed is going to have to hike.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So they've gone from under 7% to up to 7.5% now. And That's something that like we're not seeing in the monthly housing data yet because it comes out with like a month lag. But we're very much expecting to see in upcoming reports on housing that this is just going to be another hammer blow for a market that was already severely depressed because rates were so high even before this latest mortgage rate shock.

study.one_liner_ko: AI 투자 붐과 주식·집값 상승 덕에 미국 경제 성장은 강한데, 고물가·고금리 속에 일자리와 집이 없는 중산층은 소외되어 소비심리는 바닥인 'K자형' 경제를 짚는 에피소드.
summary_ko: 성장 지표는 좋지만 소비심리는 최악 수준이다. 일자리·집이 있는 사람은 잘 지내고, 없는 사람은 아메리칸 드림의 기본 요소에서 소외된 상태라 두 그룹으로 갈린다.
경제의 핵심 동력은 AI 데이터센터 투자 붐이다. 소비는 주식 상승의 수혜를 입은 고소득층이 이끄는 좁은 성장이며, 붐이 언제까지 가느냐가 최대 변수다.
CPI는 전년 대비 3.7% 올랐고(주로 에너지), 이란 전쟁 이후 실질임금은 계속 하락했다. 그런데도 기업은 비용을 소비자에게 전가하고 소비자는 계속 지출한다. 이를 'shrugflation'이라 부른다.
가계부채는 팬데믹 때 풀린 돈 덕에 줄고 있지만, 빚이 있는 사람들은 고금리로 연체율이 오르고 있다. 모기지 금리는 7%대 중반으로 뛰어 주택시장은 더 얼어붙고, 건설사는 고급 주택 쪽으로 옮겨가고 있다.
S&P는 연초 대비 12% 이상 올랐지만 AI·에너지 종목에 집중되어 있고, 금리에 민감한 주택·자동차 관련주는 부진하다. 주식시장에서도 K자형 분화가 나타난다.
중간선거를 앞두고 공화당 지지층의 심리도 트럼프 1기보다 낮다. 관세와 전쟁이 물가에 직결되기 때문이다. 연준의 추가 인상은 이미 시장에 반영되어 모기지 금리를 밀어올렸다.
study.summary_en: So this Big Take episode asks why the US economy looks strong on paper while people feel terrible about it. Basically, it's a split economy. If you have a job, a house, or stocks, you're doing fine, thanks largely to the AI data center boom. If you don't, you're kind of locked out. Inflation hit 3.7 percent, mostly because of energy prices from the Iran war, and real wages are falling, yet people keep spending. Someone called it shrugflation. Mortgage rates are up past seven percent, so housing is stuck, and the stock market rally is really narrow. If the AI boom fizzles out, a lot of this unravels.

expressions.quote: On the face of it, there are lots of positive things happening
expressions.nuance_ko: 뒤에 반전('but…')이 올 것을 예고하는 표현이다. 숫자나 첫인상을 인정한 뒤 더 깊은 문제를 꺼낼 때 쓴다. 패널이나 회의에서 논지를 전환할 때 유용하다.
examples: On the face of it, the deal looks great, but I'd read the fine print.
On the face of it, the restaurant has five stars, but half the reviews sound fake.
On the face of it, we hit our targets. The problem is how we got there.

similar.example: At first glance the numbers add up, but something feels off.
Superficially, the two plans are the same.

expressions.quote: you're kind of locked out because the hiring rate is also extremely low
expressions.nuance_ko: 원래 열쇠 없이 문밖에 갇힌 상태를 뜻하며, 비유적으로 구조적 장벽 때문에 시장·기회에 접근하지 못하는 상황에 쓴다. 'locked out of the housing market'가 대표 조합이다.
examples: A lot of young people feel locked out of the city because rents are insane.
Smaller players got locked out of the contract by the big firms.
I got locked out of my account right before the deadline.

similar.example: Families are getting priced out of neighborhoods they grew up in.
She was shut out of the negotiations from the start.

expressions.quote: I'm hearing on balance a bit more red flashing lights than green ones
expressions.nuance_ko: 장단점을 다 따져 본 뒤 결론을 내릴 때 쓴다. 'overall'보다 신중하고 균형 잡힌 인상을 주며, 의견을 정리하는 문장 앞에 붙이면 좋다.
examples: On balance, I think we should take the offer.
The trip was stressful, but on balance I'm glad we went.
On balance, the new office layout works better than the old one.

similar.example: All things considered, it went pretty well.
Weighing it all up, I'd stay put for another year.

expressions.quote: it kind of all comes down to this AI data center build-out
expressions.nuance_ko: 복잡한 논의를 하나의 핵심 요인으로 압축할 때 쓴다. 'It all comes down to X'는 토론에서 논지를 정리하는 강력한 문장 틀이다. 구어에서 'kind of all'을 끼워 부드럽게 만들기도 한다.
examples: It all comes down to whether the client trusts us.
Choosing between the two apartments comes down to commute time.
At the end of the day, it comes down to who wants it more.

similar.example: The whole argument boils down to money.
The launch hinges on one approval.

expressions.quote: businesses are able to pass those costs along to consumers
expressions.nuance_ko: 기업이 늘어난 비용을 가격 인상으로 고객에게 넘기는 것을 말한다. 'pass on'이라고도 한다. 가격결정력을 논할 때 자주 나오는 비즈니스 표현이다.
examples: The airline passed the fuel costs along to passengers with a surcharge.
Our supplier is passing the tariff along to us, and we can't absorb it.
Can the café pass the higher rent along, or will customers walk?

similar.example: They didn't want to pass on the cost to loyal customers.
We decided to eat the cost this quarter.

expressions.quote: that's really keeping things afloat at a time when
expressions.nuance_ko: 배가 가라앉지 않게 떠 있게 한다는 이미지로, 위기 속에서 무너지지 않게 받쳐 주는 요인을 가리킨다. 'at a time when…'과 함께 쓰면 대비가 선명해진다. 주어를 바꿔 'keep the business afloat'처럼 쓰기도 한다.
examples: Weekend catering is what's keeping the restaurant afloat right now.
My side gig kept me afloat during the layoffs.
A small loan from her parents kept things afloat until sales picked up.

similar.example: We're barely staying above water this month.
Subsidies are propping up the whole industry.

expressions.quote: you also have to take into account the wealth effect
expressions.nuance_ko: 논거에 빠진 변수를 덧붙일 때 쓰는 말이다. 'you also have to…'로 시작하면 상대 주장에 정중하게 보완 논점을 제기하는 효과가 있다. 'consider'보다 변수를 계산에 넣는다는 느낌이 강하다.
examples: You have to take into account the time difference when scheduling the call.
Did they take inflation into account when they set the budget?
If you take traffic into account, the cheaper flight isn't worth it.

similar.example: Factor in the commute and the salary looks less impressive.
Bear in mind that it's peak season.

expressions.quote: because they're already priced into the market
expressions.nuance_ko: 기대되는 사건이 이미 가격에 반영되어 실제 발생해도 큰 반응이 없다는 뜻이다. 금융 밖에서도 '다들 이미 예상했다'는 의미로 쓴다. 'It's already priced in.'은 짧고 강력한 한마디다.
examples: The bad earnings were already priced in, so the stock barely moved.
Everyone expected the delay. It's priced in.
Honestly, the price hike was priced in by the time they announced it.

similar.example: The cost increase is already baked in to our forecast.
The market has fully discounted that risk.

expressions.quote: another hammer blow for a market that was already severely depressed
expressions.nuance_ko: 이미 약한 대상에 가해지는 결정적 타격을 말한다. 뉴스·분석 톤으로 'deal a hammer blow to', 'a hammer blow for'가 자주 쓰인다. 'another'와 함께 쓰면 타격이 누적되는 느낌이 난다.
examples: The cancellation was a hammer blow for the small town's economy.
Losing our biggest client was a real hammer blow.
The injury is another hammer blow for a team that's struggling.

similar.example: The recall was a body blow to the brand.
Getting passed over again was a kick in the teeth.

expressions.quote: If the AI boom fizzles out, then everything is going to be going down
expressions.nuance_ko: 처음엔 기세가 좋았지만 극적인 붕괴 없이 서서히 동력을 잃는 것을 가리킨다. 'collapse'보다 약하고 맥 빠지는 어감이다. 열기·붐·계획·관계 등에 두루 쓴다.
examples: The protest fizzled out after a couple of days.
Our gym motivation always fizzles out by February.
I worry the new initiative will just fizzle out once the CEO loses interest.

similar.example: The conversation petered out around midnight.
The rally ran out of steam after lunch.

expressions.quote: has been talking up some encouraging recent wage growth numbers
expressions.nuance_ko: 실제보다 더 좋아 보이게 홍보·강조한다는 약간 냉소적인 뉘앙스가 있다. 정치인이나 기업이 자기 성과를 선전할 때 자주 쓴다. 반대 개념은 'talk down'이다.
examples: The company keeps talking up its new product before anyone's seen it.
He talked up the job so much that I expected a lot more.
Politicians love to talk up good numbers right before an election.

similar.example: The mayor touted the new park as a big win.
They played up the discount and played down the fees.

expressions.quote: from your perch covering the U.S. economy and the Fed
expressions.nuance_ko: 높은 자리에서 전체를 조망하는 이미지로, 전문 분야나 직책이 주는 관찰 시야를 가리킨다. 인터뷰에서 상대의 전문성을 인정하며 질문할 때 우아하게 쓸 수 있다. 'from where you sit'과 비슷하다.
examples: From your perch in sales, what are you hearing from customers?
From his perch as a bartender, he sees the whole neighborhood.
What does the market look like from your perch in Singapore?

similar.example: From where you sit, is the team ready?
From my vantage point, morale is low.

vocab.example: After the layoffs, there was a general sense of retrenchment across the company.
Credit card delinquency has been creeping up for months.
After the crash, a lot of households spent years deleveraging.
The rally lacks breadth. Only a handful of stocks are driving it.
Their house saw huge appreciation over the last decade.
Rising prices are slowly eroding my savings.
The hyperscalers are spending billions on new server farms.
Stress levels have been elevated at work all month.

warmup.q: Do you feel like the economy in your country or city is doing better or worse than the headlines suggest? Why?
warmup.hint_ko: 주변 체감(물가, 월세, 취업)과 뉴스 속 지표를 비교해 보고 개인 경험을 곁들여 설명.

warmup.q: What's one everyday price that has really surprised you lately, and how have you adjusted?
warmup.hint_ko: 커피, 외식, 월세 등 구체적 사례와 소비 행동 변화(대체, 절약, 그냥 지출)를 언급.

opinion.q: The hosts say growth can be strong while sentiment is weak. Which do you trust more as a signal of how an economy is really doing: hard data or how people feel?
opinion.hint_ko: GDP·고용 같은 지표의 한계, 체감 경기의 정보 가치, 평균과 분포의 차이(K자형)를 들어 입장 정리.

opinion.q: If a growth story depends on one narrow driver like AI investment, how worried should we be?
opinion.hint_ko: 집중 리스크, 붐이 꺼질 때 파급 경로, 과거 유사 사례, 그래도 지속될 수 있는 이유를 균형 있게.

debate.q: Should central banks keep raising rates even if it hits the middle class hardest through mortgages and car loans?
debate.for: Inflation erodes everyone's purchasing power, and letting it become entrenched hurts the middle class more in the long run. Rate hikes are the only tool that works.
debate.against: Hikes hit people with debt and those trying to buy a first home, while the wealthy with stocks and cash are barely affected. When the inflation comes from a supply shock like energy, higher rates don't fix the cause and deepen the split.

debate.q: Is 'shrugflation' a sign of a resilient consumer or a warning sign?
debate.for: Consumers keep spending despite higher prices, showing real strength from jobs and wealth effects that keeps the economy out of recession.
debate.against: Spending is concentrated among higher earners, while sentiment and real wages are falling. Strong demand also keeps inflation elevated, so it may be storing up trouble.

roleplay.scenario: You're on a panel at an industry conference discussing why strong economic data doesn't match how people feel. The moderator pushes you to give a clear, balanced view and to say what you'd watch next.
roleplay.your_role: Economist or analyst on the panel, who needs to explain the gap between growth and sentiment
roleplay.partner_role: Skeptical moderator who challenges your claims and asks for concrete takeaways
goals: Frame the argument with 'on the face of it…' and 'on balance…' and use 'it all comes down to…' to name the key driver.
Explain one mechanism using 'pass costs along', 'priced in' or 'locked out of'.
Name one risk, using 'fizzle out' or 'hammer blow', and say what you'd monitor.

useful_phrases.phrase: On the face of it, the numbers look fine, but…
It really comes down to one question.
You also have to take X into account.
It can be true that A, and also true that B.
useful_phrases.ko: A도 사실이고 B도 사실일 수 있다.

useful_phrases.phrase: That's definitely something we need to keep an eye on.

shadowing.reason_ko: 'You get a job, you get a house, you get a car'의 병렬 리듬과 'growth can be strong, but sentiment can be weak'의 대조 구조가 핵심 논지를 간결하게 요약하는 좋은 모델.
'even when…', 'we have X, but we also have Y', 'as long as…'로 인과를 쌓아 올리는 논리 전개. 원인 분석을 말할 때 그대로 쓸 수 있다.
'It can be true that… And also true that…'로 두 사실을 병치하고 리스크를 결론으로 잇는 패턴. 패널에서 균형 잡힌 반론을 할 때 유용.

difficulty.note_ko: 대화체지만 경제 용어(CPI, deleveraging, delinquency 등)가 많고 속도가 빠르다. 'right?', 'kind of' 같은 구어 필러와 화자 교대가 잦아 구어 담론 표지 연습에 좋다.

translations_sent.0-0: 블룸버그 오디오 스튜디오, 팟캐스트, 라디오, 뉴스.

translations_sent.15-15: 하지만 좋지 않은 신호들도 있어요. 수요일에 나온 물가 데이터도 그중 하나인데, CPI가 작년보다 3.7퍼센트 올랐고, 대부분 에너지 비용 때문이었습니다.
translations_sent.16-16: 크리스티나, 당신은 비즈니스위크에서 글로벌 경제 보도를 편집하고 계시죠.
translations_sent.17-17: 지금 경제에서 녹색 신호는 뭐고 적색 신호는 뭐라고 보세요?
translations_sent.18-18: 음, 녹색 신호는 인공지능에 대한 이 거대한 투자 물결에서 나오는 동력이 여전히 많다는 거예요.
translations_sent.19-19: 그리고 소비자들은 사람들이 예상했던 것보다 몇 년째 더 탄탄하게 버텨 왔고요.
translations_sent.20-20: 적색 신호는 여러 경제 주체들에게 돈이 점점 더 비싸지고 있다는 거예요.
translations_sent.21-21: 그래서 미국은 더 높은 조달 비용에 직면해 있고요.
translations_sent.22-22: 일부 하이퍼스케일러와 이 모든 데이터센터를 지으려는 기업들에도 영향을 주고 있어요.
translations_sent.23-23: 물론 물가도 그렇죠. 도널드 트럼프가 통제하겠다고, 혹은 통제하려고 시도하겠다며 내세웠던 생활비가 계속 오르고 있어요.
translations_sent.24-24: 여론조사를 보면 그게 사람들을 화나게 하고 있다는 걸 알 수 있고요.
translations_sent.25-25: 그리고 올해 이맘때쯤이면 주택 시장이 좀 풀리기 시작할 거라고 기대했던 것 같아요.
translations_sent.26-26: 그런데 그것도 분명 좋은 방향으로 가고 있지 않아요.
translations_sent.27-27: 알겠습니다. 종합하면 녹색보다 적색 경고등이 좀 더 많이 보이는 걸로 들리네요.
translations_sent.28-28: 맷은 어때요? 미국 경제와 연준을 취재하는 위치에서요.
translations_sent.30-30: 네, 크리스티나가 말한 것에 상당 부분 동의해요.
translations_sent.31-31: 저한테는 결국 다 AI 데이터센터 구축으로 귀결되는 것 같아요.
translations_sent.32-32: 그게 계속되는 한, 상황은 꽤 자생적인 방식으로 지금 가던 대로 계속 갈 수 있어요.
translations_sent.33-33: 소비 지출이 꽤 강했는데, 상당 부분은 고소득 소비자들 덕분이라고 봐요. AI 붐이 끌어올린 주가 상승의 혜택을 보고 있는 사람들이죠.
translations_sent.34-34: 그러니까 성장의 원천이 좁긴 하지만, 당분간은 꽤 괜찮은 원천이긴 해요.
translations_sent.36-36: 바로 이번 주에도 주식시장에서 약간의 혼란이 보이고 있어요.
translations_sent.37-37: 이럴 때 늘 나오는 질문은, 이게 일시적인 숨 고르기인가, 아니면 투자자들이 이 흐름이 지속될 기간에 대한 전망을 실제로 앞당기고 있는 건가 하는 거예요.
translations_sent.38-38: 많은 이코노미스트들은 이 흐름이 2027년이나 2028년까지 이어질 거라고 볼 거예요.
translations_sent.39-39: 하지만 물론 그건 예측하는 게 사실상 불가능한 일이죠.
translations_sent.41-41: 그럼 이번 주와 지난주에 나온 경제 데이터를 좀 더 파고들어 볼게요.
translations_sent.42-42: 물가 데이터로 CPI가 3.7퍼센트 올랐다는 게 나왔고, 임금 상승 데이터도 나왔어요.
translations_sent.43-43: 트럼프 행정부는 제조업이나 건설업 같은 블루칼라 일자리의 최근 임금 상승률이 고무적이라고 계속 강조해 왔는데요.
translations_sent.46-46: 네, 지금 보이는 일자리 증가와 임금 상승의 상당 부분은 재화 생산 쪽에서 나오고 있어요.
translations_sent.47-47: 그리고 저를 포함해 많은 사람들이 그것 역시 AI 구축이 이끌고 있다고 추정해요.
translations_sent.49-49: 그 데이터센터에 들어가는 장비를 만드는 제조업도 활발하고요.
translations_sent.50-50: 그게 크리스티나가 말했듯 주택 시장이 아주 안 좋은 시기에 경제를 떠받치고 있는 거예요.
translations_sent.51-51: 원래 그런 업종의 일자리 증가는 주택 쪽에서 나오거든요.
translations_sent.52-52: 그런 업종들이 데이터센터 덕분에 주택 부진을 무난히 헤쳐 나가고 있는 거죠.
translations_sent.54-54: 서비스 쪽에서 눈에 띄는 건 단연 헬스케어예요.
translations_sent.55-55: 지난 몇 년간 일자리 증가를 이끈 주된 동력이었죠.
translations_sent.57-57: 그게 좀 걱정스러운 게, 헬스케어 일자리 증가라는 동력을 잃으면 남는 게 별로 없거든요.
translations_sent.58-58: 그래서 분명히 계속 주시해야 할 부분이에요.
translations_sent.59-59: 그리고 이번 주에 발표된 노동통계국 데이터에 따르면 주간 평균 소득과 시간당 평균 소득이 전월 대비 약 0.5퍼센트 줄었고, 작년보다도 낮아졌습니다.
translations_sent.61-61: 물론 지금은 다들 실질임금이 어떻게 움직이는지 보면서 소비자들이 지출을 줄일지 가늠하고 있고, 그게 우려되는 부분이에요. 연료 가격이 워낙 불안정했고, 물가도 다시 하락세로 돌아설 것처럼 보였거든요.
translations_sent.62-62: 그런데 이번 달에 이 새 수치가 나오면서 전망이 덜 희망적으로 보여요.
translations_sent.64-64: 그리고 이란 전쟁이 그 가장 큰 요인 중 하나고요.
translations_sent.65-65: 이란 전쟁이 시작된 뒤로 에너지 가격이 급등하면서 올해 내내 실질임금이 줄어드는 걸 봐 왔고, 이제는 물가 상승이 더 넓게 번지는 모습이에요. 높은 에너지 가격이 다른 재화와 서비스 가격으로 스며들고 있기 때문일 수 있죠.
translations_sent.66-66: 그런데 동시에 소비 지출은 여전히 꽤 강해요.
translations_sent.67-67: 그건 기업들이 그 비용을 소비자에게 전가할 수 있다는 뜻이죠.
translations_sent.68-68: 소비자들은 가격이 오르고 구매력이 깎이는 와중에도 여전히 그 가격을 기꺼이 내고 계속 사고 있어요.
translations_sent.69-69: 그래서 저는 물가를 끌어올리는 공급 충격도 있지만, 이 모든 걸 계속 굴러가게 하는 강한 수요도 있다는 얘기라고 봐요.
translations_sent.70-70: 그리고 그렇게 강한 수요가 이어지는 한, 그 자체로 물가를 높게 유지시킬 가능성이 있어요.
translations_sent.71-71: 새로운 말을 만들어내는 재주가 있는 카일라 스캔런이 이번 주에 신조어를 하나 내놨어요.
translations_sent.73-73: 그리고 저는 많은 소비자들이 행동하는 모습을 설명하는 데 꽤 좋은 표현이라고 생각했어요. 여론조사나 설문에서는 물가 때문에 힘들다고 말하거든요.
translations_sent.74-74: 돈 사정이 빠듯하다고 하면서도, 많은 소득 계층에서 계속 소비를 하고 있죠.
translations_sent.75-75: 그리고 맷이 말했듯이, 주식 가치가 치솟고 전국 여러 지역에서 집값이 계속 오르면서 생기는 자산 효과도 감안해야 해요.
translations_sent.76-76: 네, 소비 지출 데이터는 정말 놀라울 정도예요.
translations_sent.77-77: 미국의 실제 소비 지출은 2분기에 16조 7,900억 달러로 사상 최고치를 기록했는데, 소비자심리지수는 사상 최저치이거나 그 근처에 머물러 있어요.
translations_sent.78-78: 분명 어느 정도는 어깨를 으쓱하며 넘기고 있는 거겠지만, 이걸 어떻게 설명하시겠어요?
translations_sent.79-79: 사람들이 자신의 재정 상황을 평가할 때 보통 고려하는 요인들을 생각해 보면, 일자리를 잃을지 모른다는 우려가 커졌다는 데이터가 지금 나와 있어요.
translations_sent.80-80: 그리고 AI와 관련해서는, 그런 게 배경에서 계속 진행되면서 사람들의 심리에 영향을 주고 있고, 그걸 무시하기는 어렵다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.82-82: 그래서 본인 일자리는 걱정하지 않더라도, 제가 본 인터뷰 중에 아주 인상적인 게 있었는데요, 공화당 지지 주들을 돌면서 지난 선거에서 트럼프에게 투표한 사람들과 이야기하는 내용이었어요.
translations_sent.83-83: 그런데 나이 드신 베이비붐 세대 남성 한 분이 이렇게 말하더라고요. 손녀가 걱정이라고요.
translations_sent.84-84: 대학을 졸업했는데 일자리를 못 구하고 있다는 거죠.
translations_sent.85-85: 그러니까 모든 데이터로 볼 때 꽤 괜찮은 위치에 있는 세대조차도, 자기 주변의 가까운 사람들 때문에 걱정을 하는 거예요.
translations_sent.86-86: 그리고 이런 모든 것들이 심리에는 반영되는데, 객관적인 경제 지표에는 반영되지 않는다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.88-88: 그리고 소비뿐 아니라 미국인들은 돈을 많이 빌리는 사람들이기도 합니다.
translations_sent.89-89: 물론 최근 뉴욕 연준에서 나온 데이터를 보면 가계부채가 지금은 오히려 정체되고 있다고 해요.
translations_sent.94-94: 결국 핵심은, 지금 경제가 부채보다 더 빠르게 성장하고 있다는 거예요.
translations_sent.95-95: 예를 들어 소비자 신용을 GDP 대비 비중으로 보면, 사실상 26~27년 만의 최저 수준이에요. 그만큼 광범위한 부채 축소가 있었던 거죠.
translations_sent.96-96: 그리고 그 상당 부분은 팬데믹 기간에 수표 형태로 풀린 돈과 확대된 실업보험 급여 덕분이라고 생각해요.
translations_sent.97-97: 그 시기에 가장 놀라운 경제적 사실 중 하나는, 팬데믹 경기침체 중에 가계 소득이 오히려 늘었다는 거예요. 전에는 한 번도 없었던 일이죠.
translations_sent.98-98: 그리고 그건 전부 정부가 경제에 쏟아부은 돈 때문이에요.
translations_sent.99-99: 덕분에 많은 사람들이 빚을 갚을 수 있었죠.
translations_sent.100-100: 그게 큰 반등 효과로 나타났다고 봐요.
translations_sent.101-101: 그래서 그 긴 여파가 아직 남아서 부채를 원래보다 낮게 유지해 주고 있는 거예요.
translations_sent.102-102: 동시에, 빚이 있는 사람들은 점점 더 상환이 밀리고 있는 상황이기도 해요.
translations_sent.103-103: 그래서 부채 규모 자체는 비교적 작은 기반인데도 연체율은 오르고 있습니다.
translations_sent.104-104: 그리고 그 상당 부분은 지금의 아주 높은 금리 때문인 게 분명하죠.
translations_sent.105-105: 그러니까 빚이 없으면 지금 아주 잘 지내고 있는 거고요.
translations_sent.107-107: 잠시 후에 매트, 크리스티나와 나눈 대화를 이어가겠습니다.
translations_sent.108-108: 정말 오랜만에 구매자 우위 시장이 됐습니다.
translations_sent.110-110: 파는 사람이 사는 사람보다 많아지기 시작했습니다.
translations_sent.111-111: 하지만 동시에 모기지 금리가 너무 높아서 주택 시장이 얼어붙고 있는 모습도 보고 있어요.
translations_sent.112-112: 레드핀의 9월 데이터에 따르면 매매 계약 대기 물량은 2014년 이후 최저였습니다. 완전히 다른 얘기였던 2020년 팬데믹 초반은 제외하고요.
translations_sent.113-113: 크리스티나, 주택 시장에서는 어떤 걸 보고 계시고, 지금 상황을 어떻게 설명하시겠어요?
translations_sent.114-114: 모기지 금리가 너무 올라서, 진짜 현금 구매자나 집을 줄여서 가려는 사람들만 진입할 수 있는 수준이 됐다고 생각해요.
translations_sent.115-115: 그리고 제가 최근에 편집한 부동산 기사 중에, 여러 지역을 살펴봤는데요, 정부가 첫 집 마련용 주택 건설을 밀어주는 몇몇 주를 빼면 건설업체들도 그 부문에서 빠져나와 고급 시장으로 옮겨가고 있어요.
translations_sent.116-116: 그래서 미국에서는 지난 몇 년간 어떤 자동차가 만들어지고 어떤 집이 지어지는지에 대한 이야기가 있는 것 같아요.
translations_sent.117-117: 고소득 소비자를 우선시하겠다는 거죠. 마진도 거기에 있고 회복력도 거기에 있으니까요.
translations_sent.118-118: 그럼 이제 주식 시장 이야기로 넘어가 볼게요. 주식 시장이 아주 좋거든요.
translations_sent.120-120: 물론 트럼프 행정부가 중간선거를 앞두고 계속 내세우고 있는 큰 경제 성과 중 하나죠.
translations_sent.122-122: 네, 당연히 AI가 가장 큰 이야기죠.
translations_sent.124-124: 그리고 AI 붐에 공급하는 산업재 기업들 같은 곳으로도 그 효과가 퍼지고 있는 걸 볼 수 있죠.
translations_sent.125-125: 또 다른 큰 이야기는 당연히 에너지예요. 지금 유가가 너무 높으니까요.
translations_sent.126-126: 에너지 기업들은 전쟁으로 생긴 이 상황 덕분에 돈을 많이 벌고 있어요.
